job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup we want to send Senator Whitfield's office a list of fixes. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let mining companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Below are drafting vulnerabilities in the supplied text, not verified conclusions about how a court would interpret it. Some are direct exceptions; others create enforcement gaps or litigation risk.

### Definitions and scope

1. **Section 2(1)(A)—Production threshold permits smaller operations.** Recovery of exactly 10,000 metric tons per year or less falls outside the automatic definition, even if undertaken commercially or causing serious damage. Such operations are covered only if the undefined Secretary makes a determination under section 2(1)(B).

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—Single-vessel measurement permits fleet splitting.** Companies could distribute recovery among multiple vessels, each remaining below the threshold, while collectively conducting industrial-scale mining. There is no aggregation by operator, affiliated companies, project, or mining area.

3. **Section 2(1)(A)—“Per year” is undefined.** The text does not specify a calendar year, rolling twelve-month period, or annualized rate. This creates uncertainty about when an operation crosses the threshold and whether earlier recovery becomes unlawful retroactively.

4. **Section 2(1)(A)—Tonnage measurement is unspecified.** The bill does not distinguish wet weight, dry weight, contained mineral weight, or commercially usable material. Operators could dispute the calculation or exclude discarded material and sediment despite the ecological disturbance involved.

5. **Section 2(1)(A)—Recovery-based definition omits damaging preliminary activities.** Prospecting, seabed excavation, collector testing, sediment removal, and other disturbance may occur without recovery above the threshold. The definition also does not expressly reach processing, waste discharge, or disposal associated with mining.

6. **Section 2(1)(A)—Vessel-based definition may exclude other mining systems.** Recovery through fixed platforms, seabed installations, pipelines, or distributed robotic systems may not clearly constitute recovery “by a single vessel.” Operators could structure projects around that uncertainty.

7. **Section 2(1)(A)—Depth boundary and measurement are unclear.** Mining at exactly 200 meters is excluded, and the bill does not explain how to treat projects spanning the boundary or how depth is measured. Damaging operations outside the automatic depth limit depend on section 2(1)(B).

8. **Section 2(1)(B)—“The Secretary” is not identified.** No definition specifies which department’s Secretary makes coverage determinations. This creates uncertainty about authority, implementation, and the validity of enforcement based on those determinations.

9. **Section 2(1)(B)—Discretionary expansion has no implementation deadline.** The Secretary is not required to identify comparable-risk activities or act on petitions within a specified period. Companies outside subparagraph (A) could continue while the government delays or declines to act.

10. **Section 2(1)(B)—Comparable-risk standard lacks criteria and procedures.** The text does not identify relevant ecological risks, required evidence, or whether determinations occur through rules or individual orders. Its open-ended scope—especially when coupled with criminal penalties—invites fair-notice and delegation challenges, although those challenges would not necessarily succeed.

11. **Section 2(2)—“U.S. person” excludes numerous domestic entities.** The definition omits lawful permanent residents and expressly includes only citizens and state-organized corporations, leaving LLCs, partnerships, trusts, unincorporated associations, and corporations organized under federal, District of Columbia, or territorial law outside its explicit coverage. Those entities could operate abroad without falling within the U.S.-person prohibition.

12. **Sections 2(2) and 3(a)—Foreign affiliates are not expressly covered.** Foreign-incorporated subsidiaries of U.S. companies are not themselves U.S. persons, and the bill contains no ownership-or-control rule. A domestic parent’s liability would depend on proving its own prohibited participation rather than merely its ownership of the mining subsidiary.

13. **Section 3(a)—Maritime geographic reach is not explicit.** “In the United States” does not specify treatment of the territorial sea, exclusive economic zone, continental shelf, or U.S.-flagged vessels abroad. Foreign operators could dispute coverage in offshore areas where the United States has jurisdiction over seabed resources but which are not ordinarily treated as domestic territory.

14. **Section 3(a)—“Engage in” leaves supporting conduct uncertain.** The bill does not expressly prohibit directing, financing, facilitating, contracting for, or knowingly providing equipment and services for mining. Companies could shift extraction to another entity while retaining substantial commercial involvement; existing accessory-liability rules should not be assumed to close every gap.

15. **Section 3(a)—No express ban on imports or downstream trade.** Importing, purchasing, processing, or selling minerals recovered through foreign deep-seabed mining is not expressly prohibited. Mining beyond the bill’s personal and geographic reach could therefore continue supplying U.S. markets.

### Exceptions

16. **Section 3(b)—Exploration licenses can shield commercial extraction.** The exemption attaches to mining conducted under an “exploration license,” despite the distinction between exploration and commercial exploitation. Without restrictions on authorized activities, operators could argue that large-scale recovery associated with exploration remains exempt.

17. **Section 3(b)—Qualifying licenses and issuing authorities are unspecified.** The text does not limit the exception to a particular U.S. licensing statute or agency. Operators could argue that foreign or international exploration licenses qualify, with uncertainty over what “conducted under” requires.

18. **Section 3(b)—Grandfathering has no defined operational limits.** There are no express limits on exempt production, duration, geographic expansion, license amendments, renewals, or transfers. A pre-enactment license could potentially become a vehicle for substantially expanded or successor operations.

19. **Section 3(b)—Licenses issued before enactment qualify even without existing operations.** Despite the heading “Existing Operations,” the operative text requires only a previously issued license, not mining already underway. Dormant license holders could initiate mining after enactment and claim the exemption.

20. **Section 3(c)—Environmental-assessment exception is unlimited.** There is no approval requirement, independent review, production cap, duration limit, or restriction on selling recovered minerals. Companies could characterize extensive extraction or commercial-scale trials as environmental assessment.

21. **Section 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities are not addressed.** “For the purpose of environmental assessment” does not require assessment to be the sole or primary purpose. An operation with both commercial and assessment objectives could claim the exception.

22. **Sections 3(b)–(c)—Exceptions lack verification and burden-of-proof rules.** Operators need not obtain an exemption determination or retain evidence supporting their claims, and the bill does not allocate the burden of establishing an exception. This would complicate enforcement, particularly against activities conducted far offshore.

### Registry and enforcement

23. **Sections 2(3) and 4—Registry excludes small vessels and non-vessel systems.** Vessels of exactly 5,000 gross tons or less need not register, even if they exceed the mining threshold or conduct activities designated under section 2(1)(B). Fixed installations and other non-vessel systems are also outside the registry.

24. **Sections 2(3) and 4—Vessel eligibility and responsible operator are unclear.** Neither “equipped for the recovery” nor “operator” is defined, leaving disputes over modular equipment, remote collectors, charterers, vessel managers, and project companies. The bill also specifies no gross-tonnage measurement standard.

25. **Section 4(a)—Registry jurisdiction is unspecified.** “Each covered vessel” appears unqualified, without a flag, nationality, operating-area, or jurisdictional limitation. This makes it unclear whether Congress intends registration of foreign vessels operating entirely abroad and creates practical and jurisdictional enforcement problems.

26. **Section 4—Registration and reporting deadlines are incomplete.** There is no deadline for initial registration, no requirement to register before commencing activity, and no quarterly report submission date. The text also shifts from the operator of a registered vessel to a “registered operator” without establishing operator registration.

27. **Section 4(b)—Reporting requirements are too thin to establish violations reliably.** Reports need only “describe” recovery activities, without mandatory tonnage, coordinates, depths, dates, affiliations, license information, or claimed exemptions. Operators could submit minimally informative reports that do not reveal threshold crossings or unsupported exemptions.

28. **Sections 4 and 5—Registry violations have no express penalty.** Section 5 penalizes violations of section 3 only, not failures to register or report under section 4. Other generally applicable laws might address some false statements, but the bill supplies no dedicated sanctions for noncompliance with the registry.

29. **Sections 3–5—No lead enforcement agency or general implementation authority is designated.** NOAA receives reports, but the bill does not assign responsibility for enforcing the prohibition or expressly authorize implementing regulations. Existing agency authority may help, but the text leaves major institutional responsibilities unresolved.

30. **Sections 4–5—No express inspection or evidence-gathering powers.** The bill supplies no vessel-inspection authority, records-access requirement, subpoena power, monitoring requirement, or record-retention period. Those omissions could make remote operations difficult to investigate unless other law provides sufficient authority.

31. **Section 5(a)—Civil penalty procedures and enforcement forum are unspecified.** The bill does not say who assesses penalties, whether proceedings are administrative or judicial, how penalties are collected, or how decisions are reviewed. This invites procedural disputes and may leave agencies without the intended administrative enforcement mechanism.

32. **Sections 3 and 5—No express authority for prompt preventive relief.** The bill does not specifically authorize stop-work orders, injunctions, equipment seizure, or forfeiture of recovered minerals. Existing remedies may be available, but penalties alone do not clearly provide a means to halt ongoing ecological damage.

33. **Section 5(a)—Penalty unit is uncertain.** The text establishes a maximum penalty for each day but does not specify whether separate vessels, sites, or acts generate separate daily penalties. Companies could seek treatment of numerous simultaneous operations as one daily violation.

34. **Section 5(b)—Willfulness and uncertain coverage complicate prosecutions.** Prosecutors must prove a willful violation, while coverage depends on ambiguous thresholds, exceptions, and potentially discretionary determinations. Those uncertainties could strengthen defenses based on lack of notice or lack of the required criminal intent.

35. **Sections 3–5—Foreign-operation enforcement mechanisms are absent.** Although the prohibition expressly reaches U.S. persons anywhere, the bill provides no tailored mechanism for obtaining overseas records, inspecting overseas operations, or securing compliance from foreign affiliates. Substantive extraterritorial coverage alone does not resolve those practical obstacles.

### International agreement, duration, and effective date

36. **Section 6—Negotiation obligation does not require a binding prohibition.** “Shall seek to negotiate” requires an effort, not successful conclusion, ratification, or entry into force, and “international agreement” does not expressly require a legally binding instrument. The provision therefore does not secure CADM’s stated treaty objective.

37. **Section 6—Deadline and required equivalence are ambiguous.** It is unclear whether negotiations must begin or be completed within eighteen months. Requiring prohibitions “equivalent” to section 3 may also carry the exploration and environmental-assessment exceptions into the international instrument.

38. **Section 7(a)—Safety finding lacks a defined standard or report process.** “Without serious harm” does not specify ecological baselines, geographic scope, cumulative effects, permanence, or acceptable scientific uncertainty. The bill also does not commission the National Academies report, specify its contents, or require Congress’s finding to match its conclusions.

39. **Sections 7(a)–(b)—Automatic sunset undermines the safety condition.** Section 7(a) suggests the prohibition lasts until Congress makes a safety finding, but section 7(b) terminates the entire Act after ten years regardless of safety. Mining could resume without a favorable report or congressional finding.

40. **Section 7(b)—Sunset creates uncertainty about surviving obligations and proceedings.** “This Act shall cease to have effect” terminates more than the prohibition and includes no express savings provision for reporting obligations, investigations, or pending enforcement. General federal savings law may preserve accrued penalties, but the bill should not leave the intended treatment of ongoing matters implicit.

41. **Sections 5(a) and 8—Penalty commencement conflicts with delayed effectiveness.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while section 8 delays the Act’s effectiveness by 180 days. This creates uncertainty about civil liability during that interval and invites objections to any attempt to penalize conduct before the prohibition takes effect.

42. **Section 8—Six-month window permits continued mining.** The prohibition itself is delayed for 180 days, allowing otherwise covered operations to continue during that period. There is no interim restriction on starting or expanding operations.

43. **Act generally—No express coordination with existing mining authorizations.** The bill does not address suspension or revocation of existing authorizations, prevent issuance of conflicting new authorizations, or conform existing seabed-mining statutes. Although an authorization would not necessarily override section 3, unresolved overlap could generate administrative confusion and litigation.
